Clinical and biochemical correction of a patient with neurodegenerative mucopolysaccharidosis IIIA using hematopoietic stem cell gene therapy
abstract: Autologous hematopoietic stem cell gene therapy (HSC-GT) is an emerging therapy for treatment-refractory neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders (LSDs). Mucopolysaccharidosis IIIA (MPSIIIA) is a devastating LSD where pathogenic variants in the gene SGSH lead to toxic heparan sulfate accumulation, inflammation, and cell death. Children present with developmental delay, neurodegeneration, and significant behavioral disturbance and die in late teens. We report 80-month outcomes for a patient with severe MPSIIIA following treatment with investigational autologous HSC-GT (OTL-201) at 30 months of age. Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) were collected from peripheral blood following mobilization with granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) and plerixafor. HSPCs were transduced with a lentiviral vector containing SGSH and the CD11b promoter. The product was infused following myeloablative conditioning with busulfan. Product engraftment was rapid, with production of sustained supra-physiological SGSH enzyme measured in leukocytes, plasma, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and reductions in substrate heparan sulfate to within the normal range in urine, plasma, and CSF. Neurocognitive outcomes on the Bayley Scale of Infant Development (BSID-III) and parent-reported outcomes showed improvements compared to natural history. This demonstrates sustained long-term efficacy and safety of HSC-GT in a patient with severe MPSIIIA, setting the scene for a phase 1/2 clinical trial in younger patients.

title: Base editing-mediated induction of stop codons in HPV18 E6/E7 for cervical cancer therapy
abstract: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomaviruses (hrHPVs) is a primary driver of cervical carcinogenesis, with the viral oncogenes E6 and E7 playing pivotal roles. Conventional nuclease-based gene-editing strategies are limited by genome-wide off-target effects and genomic perturbations associated with double-strand breaks (DSBs). To address these challenges, we developed BE-PLUS-induction of STOP codons (iSTOP), a DSB-free cytosine base-editing strategy designed to inactivate HPV18 E6/E7 through the precise installation of premature termination codons (PTCs). This strategy achieved high on-target editing efficiencies (51.00% ± 2.94% for E6 and 26.33% ± 2.62% for E7) with minimal insertion or deletion (indel) formation (undetectable for E6 and <0.1% for E7). Functional analyses demonstrated that BE-PLUS-iSTOP effectively reduced E6/E7 protein expression, resulting in robust suppression of malignant phenotypes in HPV18-positive cervical cancer cells. In a subcutaneous xenograft mouse model, intratumoral delivery of BE-PLUS-iSTOP induced extensive tumor necrosis and significantly suppressed tumor growth, with no overt systemic toxicity under the tested conditions. Collectively, these findings establish BE-PLUS-iSTOP as a precise and efficient etiology-directed therapeutic strategy for HPV18-positive cervical cancer, supporting its potential for further translational development and broadening the scope of antiviral gene therapy.

title: Broad targeting of the cell adhesion machinery: Cancer cell detachment triggered by the alpha1-oleate complex
abstract: A new approach to targeting cell adhesion in oncology was recently suggested by observations made in patients with bladder cancer. Intravesical alpha1-oleate treatment triggered rapid tumor cell detachment into the urine and a parallel reduction in tumor number and size. This study identified alpha1-oleate as a potent inhibitor of multiple cell adhesion families in shed cells and tumor biopsies from treated patients, confirmed in cellular models. Alpha1-oleate targeted claudins and focal adhesion constituents and disrupted tight junctions, focal adhesions, and adherens junctions, but gap junctions or desmosomes were not affected. The effects on cell adhesion were dose dependent, with stronger cell detachment and broader inhibition of adhesion-associated genes in patients treated with 8.5 mM of alpha1-oleate than the 1.7 mM dose. These acute and sustained effects identify cell detachment as a contributor to the anti-tumor effects observed clinically. AlphaFold predictions identified claudins and the focal adhesion targeting (FAT) domain of focal adhesion kinase (FAK) as potential alpha1-oleate targets, but inhibitors of claudin and FAK phosphorylation showed less potent effects than alpha1-oleate on cell detachment. The broad effect of alpha1-oleate on the cell adhesion machinery is unprecedented and suggests that therapeutic targeting of the cell adhesion machinery by alpha1-oleate should be further explored.

title: Novel HIV fusion-inhibitory lipopeptides exhibit dramatically improved activity against resistant mutants
abstract: LP-98 is a potent HIV fusion-inhibitory lipopeptide but displays reduced activity against resistant mutants. In this study, we rationally designed a group of new lipopeptides by adding different lengths of gp41 pocket-binding sequence into the N terminus of LP-98. It was found that a single pocket-inserting residue Ile124 critically determined the anti-HIV activity, whereas incorporation of additional pocket-inserting residues Trp120 and Trp117 generated lipopeptides with greatly reduced activity. As indicated by LP-101 and LP-108, while Ile124-modified lipopeptides maintained or improved the inhibitory activity of LP-98 against divergent HIV and simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) isolates, they had dramatically increased potencies on the resistant mutants. In both the HIV-infected humanized mice and SIV-infected rhesus macaques, LP-101 efficiently suppressed viral replication below detection limits. Mechanically, Ile124-modified lipopeptides exhibited greatly enhanced binding affinity with a target-mimic peptide N44. We determined the crystal structure of LP-101 bound to N44, revealing its N-terminal residues penetrating deeper into the gp41 pocket, forming enhanced interactions with the target site. Molecular dynamics simulations also revealed that its flexible N terminus enables adaptive binding to the wild-type and resistant mutants, with improved binding free energies. Therefore, our data inform the structure-activity relationship of this class of HIV fusion inhibitors and offer new candidates for drug development.

title: Targeting Telomerase with an HLA Class II-Restricted TCR for Cancer Immunotherapy
abstract: T cell receptor (TCR)-engineered T cell therapy is a promising cancer treatment approach. Human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) is overexpressed in the majority of tumors and a potential target for adoptive cell therapy. We isolated a novel hTERT-specific TCR sequence, named Radium-4, from a clinically responding pancreatic cancer patient vaccinated with a long hTERT peptide. Radium-4 TCR-redirected primary CD4+ and CD8+ T cells demonstrated in vitro efficacy, producing inflammatory cytokines and killing hTERT+ melanoma cells in both 2D and 3D settings, as well as malignant, patient-derived ascites cells. Importantly, T cells expressing Radium-4 TCR displayed no toxicity against bone marrow stem cells or mature hematopoietic cells. Notably, Radium-4 TCR+ T cells also significantly reduced tumor growth and improved survival in a xenograft mouse model. Since hTERT is a universal cancer antigen, and the very frequently expressed HLA class II molecules presenting the hTERT peptide to this TCR provide a very high (>75%) population coverage, this TCR represents an attractive candidate for immunotherapy of solid tumors.

title: Retraction Notice to: Gas5 Exerts Tumor-suppressive Functions in Human Glioma Cells by Targeting miR-222
APOBEC3 knockout in lentiviral packaging cells improves therapeutic transgene sequence fidelity
abstract: hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, we detected a disproportionately high frequency of cytosine-to-thymine mutations. We, therefore, hypothesized that blocking the APOBEC3 family of antiviral cytosine deaminases would improve transgene fidelity. We demonstrated that CRISPR-Cas9-mediated knockout of the APOBEC3 locus in HEK293T packaging lines reduced total lentiviral transgene mutations by over 90%. Conversely, disrupting the murine leukemia virus's APOBEC3 defenses caused an approximately 30-fold increase in C/G-to-T/A mutations. Furthermore, we determined that APOBEC3 knockout is compatible with a multi-gene knockout packaging line designed to enhance titer. This novel combination resulted in "CHAI" (CRISPRed HEK293Ts with Antiviral Inhibition), a HEK293T-based cell line that produces high-titer lentiviral vectors with near-perfect transgene fidelity.

title: Planning advanced therapy trials for Huntington’s disease: Ethical considerations
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a relentlessly progressive genetic disorder characterized by cognitive, behavioral, and physical impairments. The lack of effective treatments, early onset of symptoms, and high rates of suicide reflect a disease of significant human suffering. The ethical imperative to pursue disease modifying treatments with gene and stem cell therapies-collectively referred to as advanced therapeutic medicinal products (ATMPs)-is therefore sound. Recent gene therapy trials have generated international attention and widespread hope in the HD community; however, gene and stem cell therapies are fraught with ethical challenges and complexity. Genetic discrimination, trial design challenges (especially the use of surgical placebos), and the risk for therapeutic misconception need careful consideration while broader concerns relating to justice and equity must be recognized by researchers and funders alike. This paper will provide those involved in gene therapy trials and other advanced therapy research a comprehensive overview of the ethical issues.

title: Decoupling reactogenicity from efficacy enables safer mRNA vaccines, AAV gene delivery, and in vivo base editing
abstract: Nucleic acid therapeutics, including mRNA vaccines, genome editors, and viral vectors, are constrained by acute innate reactogenicity that limits dosing flexibility, tissue targeting, and safety. Here, we identify a conserved early innate inflammatory program, peaking approximately 6 h after administration, that governs reactogenicity across mRNA-formulated lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), adenoviral vectors, and AAV9. Using pharmacological and biochemical probes, we show that this program is driven predominantly by nucleic acid cargo sensing, rather than lipid components, and is mechanistically separable from antigen expression, adaptive immune priming, and in vivo genome-editing efficacy. Selective modulation of this early cytokine burst achieved here using endosomal nucleic acid-sensing suppressors markedly reduces reactogenicity in multiple mouse models while preserving humoral and cellular immunity to mRNA vaccines, maintaining transgene expression, protecting blood-brain barrier integrity during stereotactic AAV9 delivery, and mitigating LNP-associated hepatotoxicity and thrombocytopenia. These findings define a unifying innate-sensing architecture for nucleic acid therapeutics and establish that reactogenicity is not required for effective vaccination or gene delivery, enabling a broadly applicable strategy to widen the safety window of mRNA medicines, viral vectors, and in vivo genome editing.

title: Triple-AAV intein-mediated gene therapy ameliorates dystrophic phenotype in MDC1A mice
Anti-CD19-engineered exosomes enable B cell-targeted anti-BAFF mRNA delivery to alleviate lupus progression
Protein trans-splicing: Solving the challenge of gene therapy for large genes
Molecular Therapy Family Highlights
Targeting the miR-3156-3p/K+ channel axis suppresses viral release and paralysis in enterovirus D68 infection
abstract: Viruses rely on egress machinery to exit cells, a step that is crucial for their transmission. While non-enveloped RNA viruses, such as enteroviruses, are typically associated with the lytic release pathway, emerging evidence suggests they can also be packaged within vesicles for non-lytic release. However, the molecular mechanisms that regulate viral release remain unclear. Here, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in A549 cells and identified the microRNA hsa-miR-3156-1 as a critical host factor for enterovirus infection. Both the primary and mature forms of miR-3156-1 were upregulated following infection, with miR-3156-3p acting as a positive regulator of viral infection by directly targeting the 3' untranslated regions of the K + channel-associated genes KCNV1, KCNJ2, KCNK3, and KCNK5, thereby causing plasma membrane depolarization and Ca 2+ influx, which increase viral release. Pre-administration of a miR-3156-3p antagomir alleviated virus-associated acute flaccid paralysis in an ICR neonatal mouse model. Our findings reveal how the miR-3156-3p/K + channel axis controls enterovirus release, highlighting potential prophylactic targets.

title: Receptor-ligand matching for precision allogeneic NK cell cancer therapies
abstract: Allogeneic natural killer (NK) cell therapies have a favorable safety profile. NK cell cytotoxicity is the result of interactions between activating and inhibitory receptors and tumor-cell ligands expressed in the tumoral cell. This complex, donor-dependent interaction could explain variable persistence and limited durability across clinical trials. Here, we discuss an emergent framework for improving NK cell efficacy through systemic receptor-ligand matching grounded in NK licensing and donor-recipient immunogenetics, particularly KIR/HLA class I interactions, integrated with tumor ligand landscapes such as stress-induced NKG2D ligands. This review synthesizes how inhibitory and activating receptor repertoires calibrate NK functional competence, why identical KIR/HLA configurations yield context-dependent outcomes across malignancies and treatments, and how tumor immune evasion can decouple ligand expression from NK recognition. Based on this evidence hierarchy, we propose a biomarker-driven stratification framework to guide decisions on donor selection, redosing, and combination therapy. We further discuss how emerging machine learning classifiers and multiscale computational models could extend this framework to the clinical scale. Finally, we propose that the systematic incorporation of receptor-ligand immunogenetics into the design of an adoptive NK cell clinical trial is a necessary and tractable step toward improving the mechanistic interpretability, clinical development, and reproducibility of allogeneic NK cell therapies.

title: Cryo-thermal therapy reprograms myeloid cells into CCL5+ mature phenotype to increase T cell infiltration and potentiate anti-PD-1 therapy
abstract: Although immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) represented by anti-programmed death-1 (PD-1) therapy has demonstrated significant clinical benefits, its efficacy remains limited by the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Our study revealed that the combination of cryo-thermal therapy (CTT) and anti-PD-1 therapy suppresses distal tumor growth compared with either cryoablation or radiofrequency ablation combined with anti-PD-1 therapy. Mechanistically, CTT specifically induces tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α production in mature myeloid cells, triggering autocrine CCL5 secretion that recruits peripheral interferon (IFN)-γ + T cells induced by CTT in distal tumors, creating a cytokine loop in which IFN-γ derived from T cells and TNF-α derived from myeloid cells collectively promote CCL5 secretion in myeloid cells to increase effector T cell recruitment in distal tumors. After CTT, anti-PD-1 treatment amplifies this cascade by enhancing TNF-α production in T cells. The parallel activation of STAT1 by IFN-γ and nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) by TNF-α in myeloid cells converges to drive IRF7-dependent CCL5 upregulation to create a local immune-enhancing environment via CCL5-mediated recruitment of T cells. Our study demonstrates that CTT establishes an immunologically favorable TME by reprogramming immunosuppressive myeloid cells into mature myeloid cells with high CCL5 production, thereby facilitating effector T cell recruitment and providing an efficient therapeutic strategy to promote the response to anti-PD-1 therapy.

title: From splice defect to therapeutic opportunity: Insights from PRPF31
Mapping immunocompetent tissues for safer vaccines and gene therapy: A miRNA-based strategy for mRNA-LNP platforms
In this issue
Breakthroughs in cell and gene therapy: Innovations in therapeutic modalities for the CNS, targeted delivery, translation, and CMC
Sustained relief of chronic pain via a Nav1.7-targeting ASO-siRNA conjugate in rats
abstract: SUMMARY Chronic pain affects billions globally, yet safe, long-lasting, and non-addictive analgesics remain lacking. Nav1.7 is a genetically validated pain target, but traditional small molecules have repeatedly failed. Therapeutic oligonucleotides-antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and siRNAs-offer selective, durable silencing. We developed N02C0702, an ASO-siRNA conjugate (ASC), achieving robust Nav1.7 knockdown and sustained analgesia without additional delivery vehicles. N02C0702 outperformed individual ASO (N02A114) and siRNA (N02S154) moieties at mRNA and protein levels and in pain relief. In CFA-induced inflammatory pain, a single intrathecal dose exceeded naproxen and suzetrigine, while in SNL neuropathic pain, efficacy persisted up to 56 days, comparable to or surpassing pregabalin. Genome-wide RNA sequencing confirmed minimal off-target effects. N02C0702 highlights Nav1.7 as a key analgesic target and demonstrates the ASC platform’s potential for chronic pain and other CNS-related pathologies, offering durable, selective, and safe therapeutic effects.

title: An RGD-directed melittin/anti-4-1BB dual-lock prodrug safely reinvigorates robust anti-tumor immunity
abstract: The clinical application of agonist antibodies that provide a second signal for T cell activation, such as anti-4-1BB, is severely hampered by their systemic immune-related toxicity. Here, we introduce a novel dual-lock strategy, which involves the development of a prodrug comprising the melittin mutant MP5/4-1BB agonist antibody/RGD, named MmHm4R, to address this issue. MmHm4R consists of the lytic peptide MP5 and a human IgG1 hinge domain fused to the N terminus of the 4-1BB agonist antibody via cleavable peptide linkers sensitive to tumor-enriched proteinases, and RGD peptides fused to the C terminus to further enhance tumor specificity. This strategy effectively masks both MP5 and anti-4-1BB antibody in circulation, significantly reducing hemolysis and immune-related adverse events. Upon cleavage of the linkers in the tumor, MP5 and anti-4-1BB antibody are released from MmHm4R and restore their activities, resulting in significantly reduced toxicity and superior antitumor efficacy. Mechanistically, MP5 induces tumor cell lysis, enhances antigen exposure, and stimulates 4-1BB expression in intratumoral lymphocytes, thereby synergizing with anti-4-1BB antibody. Overall, our study highlights the clinical potential of the dual-lock prodrug strategy, which effectively combines the potent effects of immune agonists and tumor lytic peptides to develop safer and more effective cancer immunotherapies.

title: Dendrimer Delivered shRNA Targeting the CCL20–CCR6 Axis Suppresses Complement-Mediated Microglial Synaptic Pruning and Ameliorates Chronic Neuroinflammation After Repetitive Traumatic Brain Injury
abstract: Repetitive traumatic brain injury (rTBI) induces persistent microglial activation and chronic neuroinflammation, yet the upstream signals driving long-term synaptic injury remain unclear. In this study, we identify the CCL20-CCR6 chemokine axis as a critical regulator of sustained microglial activation and complement-dependent synaptic loss after rTBI. Proteomic profiling at 30 days post-injury (dpi) showed broad normalization of complement-linked inflammatory and synaptic pathways in the cortex and hippocampus, underscoring a mechanistic link between chemokine signaling, microglial activation, and synaptic vulnerability. To therapeutically target this axis, we developed a dendrimer-based shRNA platform (shCombo-DPX) that simultaneously silences CCL20 and CCR6. Intranasal and intravenous delivery in rTBI mice effectively reduced CCL20-CCR6 expression, attenuated chronic microgliosis and astrogliosis, and suppressed complement activation. Treatment limited microglial synaptic engulfment, preserved synaptic proteins, restored BDNF levels, and improved motor, anxiety-related, and cognitive outcomes. In microglia-neuron coculture systems, CCL20 silencing reduced LPS-induced complement signaling and prevented synaptic loss, neuronal apoptosis, and BDNF depletion. Conversely, exposure to recombinant CCL20 induced dendritic degeneration, caspase-3 activation, microglial reactivity, complement dysregulation, and synaptic injury both in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish CCL20-CCR6 as a key upstream driver of chronic complement-mediated synaptic degeneration after rTBI and support dendrimer-delivered shRNA therapy as a targeted strategy to mitigate long-term neurodegeneration.

title: Inhibition of CCN2/CTGF prevents heterotopic ossification in fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva
abstract: Heterotopic ossification (HO) is the aberrant formation of endochondral bone within soft tissues, triggered by trauma, burns, or the congenital disorder fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). In this study, we demonstrate that mesenchymal progenitors (MPs) harboring the ACVR1 wt/R206H mutation exhibit resistance to apoptosis, likely contributing to their pathological accumulation during FOP flare-ups. Transcriptomic analysis of these mutant MPs reveals dysregulation of genes associated with fibrosis and osteogenic differentiation and elevated expression of matricellular signaling proteins, most notably Ccn2/Ctgf. We further show, using both genetic and pharmacological approaches, that Ccn2 induction in ACVR1 wt/R206H MPs is driven by the cooperative interaction between SMAD1 and YAP-TEAD at the Ccn2 promoter. Osteochondrogenic specification of ACVR1 wt/R206H MPs was blocked by the CCN2-neutralizing antibody pamrevlumab. Moreover, pamrevlumab not only partially suppresses activin A-regulated extracellular matrix organization and transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) family transcriptional programs in mutant MPs but also significantly ameliorates ectopic bone formation in an FOP mouse model. Collectively, these findings identify CCN2/CTGF as a critical mediator of HO and support its inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy for FOP and disorders characterized by pathological ossification.

title: Intramuscular non-replicating Tiantan vaccinia drives antibody maturation and sterilizing protection against orthopoxvirus in mice
abstract: The global resurgence of orthopoxviruses, particularly monkeypox virus (MPXV), necessitates safe yet highly protective vaccines. Here, we systematically evaluated a non-replicating Tiantan vaccinia virus (NTV)-derived from the historically efficacious vaccinia Tiantan strain-across intramuscular (i.m.), subcutaneous (s.c.), and dose-sparing intradermal (i.d.) routes in lethal murine models. While all regimens elicited robust polyfunctional T cells, cross-neutralizing antibodies against MPXV, VTT, and ectromelia virus (ECTV), and protective immunity against standard lethal vaccinia virus (VACV)-WR and ECTV challenges, under extreme viral exposure (70 LD 50 ) and long-term challenge (16 week), only full-dose NTV-IM among the non-replicating regimens conferred complete sterilizing cross-protection, whereas the SC and dose-sparing ID regimens exhibited breakthrough virologic failure. Mechanistically, splenic transcriptomics revealed that NTV-IM uniquely enriched for a prominent germinal center (GC) transcriptional profile (marked by activation-induced cytidine deaminase [Aicda]). This GC signature was multi-dimensionally validated by RT-qPCR, flow cytometry, and immunofluorescence, confirming robust expansion of GC B cells (CD95 + GL7 + ) and highly organized follicular architecture in lymphoid organs. This optimized GC response closely correlated with superior affinity maturation and class-switch recombination, aligning with the production of the highest titers of IgG and cross-neutralizing antibodies in NTV-IM without inducing systemic inflammation. Collectively, these findings highlight route-dependent immune programming, establishing NTV-IM as a scalable, next-generation orthopoxvirus vaccine candidate.

title: Five decades of gene therapy innovation and regulation in the US and EU: A historical analysis
abstract: The development of gene therapy is characterized by expectations of patient benefits, but challenges persist, including rapid technological change and, typically, small target populations. This has thus far resulted in relatively few gene therapies reaching the market and benefiting patients. Regulation plays a central role in shaping how these challenges are addressed and how gene therapies reach patients. This study investigated how gene therapy regulatory regimes have developed in the US and EU between 1973 and 2025, and how gene therapy regulation events contributing to regulatory regime building have shaped gene therapy innovation outcomes. We conducted a scoping review of scientific literature and expert interviews, which together characterized all authorized gene therapies in the US and EU. We constructed and validated timelines of gene therapy regulation events in these regimes. Interviewees attributed observed differences in the timelines to factors specific to gene therapy regulation and to the broader medicines regulatory system. Regulatory leadership in gene therapy has shifted repeatedly between the US and the EU, reflecting differences in how each jurisdiction responds to scientific and technological uncertainty, societal risks and needs, and commercial pressure.

title: News from biotech
miR-124 delivery to the hippocampus reduces excitability, enhances neurogenesis, and affects microglia in a model of Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: MicroRNA-124 (miR-124) has been proposed as therapeutic candidate for Alzheimer's disease (AD), given its regulation of gene networks governing synaptic function, neurogenesis and inflammation. However, its functional role during early disease stages, and the cellular context-dependence of its effects, remain unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of targeted neuronal miR-124 delivery to the hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) of App NL-G-F mice. At an earlier ‘presymptomatic' stage, miR-124 reduced intrinsic excitability of mature granule neurons and induced subtle changes in dendritic architecture. Integrative transcriptomic analyses revealed that predicted miR-124 targets were enriched among downregulated genes involved in synapse organization and cell junction assembly. At the same time, miR-124 increased the number of immature neurons and microglia, indicating structural and functional remodeling of the DG. At a later ‘symptomatic' disease stage, where AD pathology is established, neuronal miR-124 supplementation reduced DG Aβ 40 and Aβ 42 levels and decreased local amyloid plaque burden, while also altering the plaque-associated microglial response. Together, these findings identify neuronal miR-124 as a context- and disease-stage-dependent regulator of the DG microenvironment and demonstrate effects extending from neuronal function to other cellular populations and local AD-associated pathology.

title: Reprogramming immunosuppressive TMEs with Salmonella-delivered sialidase and COX-2 blockade synergistically enhances cancer immunotherapy
abstract: Sialic acid is a component of the extracellular matrix that is upregulated in multiple tumors and plays critical roles in tumorigenesis and progression. Sialic acid engages sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-like lectins (Siglecs) on immune cells to suppress immune activation. Despite the potential of sialylation-targeted therapies to reactivate antitumor immunity, their clinical translation remains limited by suboptimal drug delivery systems and insufficient tumor specificity. To overcome these obstacles, we engineered a sialidase-expressing S. typhimurium and termed it SLpnanH. The engineered avirulent bacteria can express and secrete sialidase in situ upon L-arabinose induction. In highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments, SLpnanH manifests very specific tumor-targeting capabilities and expresses sialidase at high levels. This study demonstrates that engineered SLpnanH significantly mitigates the tumor immunosuppressive microenvironment and inhibits tumor growth with markedly elongated animal survival compared with control groups. Furthermore, treatment with SLpnanH promotes the infiltration and activation of CD8 + T cells and dendritic cells (DCs) in the tumor-draining lymph nodes. When combined with a selective cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitor, the therapeutic efficacy of SLpnanH was further enhanced. Collectively, these findings underscore SLpnanH as a promising candidate for cancer immunotherapy, with its antitumor efficacy significantly augmented by the adjunctive application of an FDA-approved COX-2 inhibitor.

title: Retraction Notice to: Recurrent ZNF83-E293VMutationPromotesBladder Cancer Progression through the NF-κB Pathway via Transcriptional Dysregulation of S100A8
A natural compound derivative targeting HADHA disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis and suppresses renal cell carcinoma
abstract: Metastatic renal cell carcinoma (RCC) remains a lethal malignancy, and therapeutic resistance to current targeted and immune-based therapies highlights the need for new treatment strategies. Here, we identify C18-epi-brasilibactin A (CBA) as a selective inhibitor of RCC. High-throughput screening of a compound library derived from natural products revealed that CBA potently suppresses RCC cell proliferation, while sparing normal renal epithelial and liver cells. Mechanistically, CBA induces cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, and DNA damage. Transcriptomic and functional analyses showed that CBA disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis by increasing mitochondrial mass and reactive oxygen species, indicating metabolic stress. Using proteomic approaches, we identified hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase trifunctional multienzyme complex subunit alpha (HADHA), a key enzyme in mitochondrial fatty acid β-oxidation, as a key functional mediator of CBA. Genetic depletion of HADHA phenocopied CBA effects, inducing ROS accumulation, DNA damage response, apoptosis, and growth inhibition in RCC cells. CBA treatment significantly suppressed RCC xenograft growth, without systemic toxicity. Consistently, HADHA knockdown inhibited tumor progression, whereas HADHA overexpression enhanced tumor growth, supporting a tumor-supportive role for HADHA in RCC. Together, our findings identify HADHA-dependent mitochondrial metabolism as a functional vulnerability in RCC and establish CBA as a candidate therapeutic agent for targeting metabolic dependencies in metastatic RCC.

title: Lentiviral gene therapy corrects the metabolic and immune abnormalities in purine nucleoside phosphorylase-deficient mice
abstract: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency impairs purine metabolism leading to severe T cell defects, which can be corrected by allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplant, however the associated complications are significant. Therefore, autologous gene therapy is an attractive alternative treatment option. Here, we present a third-generation self-inactivating lentiviral vector expressing the human PNP gene under the control of the elongation factor-1 alpha short promoter (LVV-EFS-PNP), which was delivered ex vivo to HSCs and was tested for its ability to correct the abnormalities in PNP-deficient (Pnp-/-) mice. The LVV-EFS-PNP vector demonstrated effective gene transfer, without jeopardizing hematopoietic colony formation in vitro. In vivo, Pnp-/- mice transplanted with Pnp-/- lineage-negative cells transduced with LVV-EFS-PNP achieved sustained correction of the immune and metabolic abnormalities, including restoration of thymocyte development, T cell proliferation, and T cell-dependent and independent antibody responses. Importantly, genotoxicity assessments demonstrated that LVV-EFS-PNP had a low transformation potential and did not significantly dysregulate gene expression signature linked to vector-induced transformation, similar to other clinically used lentiviruses. These results demonstrate the safety and efficacy of gene therapy using LVV-EFS-PNP in a pre-clinical model of PNP deficiency, providing evidence for a promising new treatment strategy.

title: IL-12-producing iPSC-derived antigen-presenting cells enhance antitumor immunity and enable off-the-shelf immunotherapy
abstract: Effective activation of cancer-reactive T cells by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) is essential for tumor elimination. However, dendritic cell (DC)-based cancer vaccines often yield inconsistent clinical outcomes due to patient-dependent variability. We established IL-12-producing proliferative myeloid cells (IL12-pMCs) from mouse induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) as a standardized APC platform. These cells stably secrete IL-12, express costimulatory molecules, and enhance the priming and expansion of antigen-specific CD8 + T cells, while also activating NK cells. Upon tumor antigen loading and in vivo administration, IL12-pMCs induced robust IFN-related gene signatures in tumors, promoted infiltration of effector cells, suppressed immunosuppressive populations, and showed potent antitumor efficacy, with further enhancement when combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). For clinical application, we generated human IL12-pMCs from iPSCs with selective HLA expression to enable antigen-specific CD8 + T cell priming while minimizing alloreactivity. This system offers a potent, off-the-shelf APC platform for next-generation cancer immunotherapy.

title: The allogeneic eDN70(-) CAR-T Cells Without TCR or MHC Editing Exhibit Enhanced Persistence and Function
abstract: Allogeneic CAR-T therapy offers an "off-the-shelf" alternative to autologous CAR-T, but faces graft-versus-host rejection (GVH) and host-versus-graft rejection (HVG). Conventional TCR/MHC elimination compromises persistence and increase NK susceptibility. Here, we developed a next-generation UCAR-T strategy that avoids TCR/MHC disruption while addressing donor-cell alloreactivity and host-mediated rejection. First, we eliminated CD4/CD8 to reduce alloreactivity while preserving TCR integrity and potentially TCR/CD3-mediated fitness, although in vivo xGvHD protection remains to be determined. In parallel, we identified CD70 as a marker selectively upregulated on alloreactive immune cells, enabling targeted removal of HVG-driving subsets. Because CD70 is also induced during T-cell activation and further enhanced following CD4/CD8 knockout, we additionally deleted CD70 to prevent fratricide, generating a CD4/CD8/CD70 triple-negative UCAR-T backbone (eDN70(-) UCAR-T). As proof-of-concept, we incorporated both CD19- and CD70-targeting CARs to generate eDN70(-)19/70CAR-T cells, which showed superior expansion, reduced exhaustion, and greater resistance to HVG pressure. Furthermore, these cells demonstrated durable tumor control and robust recall responses in vivo, with preliminary tissue-level safety from the high-dose study. Collectively, our findings establish eDN70(-) UCAR-T cells as a versatile platform capable of overcoming the persistence limitations of current allogeneic CAR-T therapies, with the CD19/CD70 dual-target configuration serving as a representative implementation of this strategy.

title: Beyond Excitotoxicity: Glutamate-Independent Mechanisms Underlie Noise-Induced Synaptopathy and Compromise Gene Therapy for Hereditary Deafness
abstract: Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is classically attributed to glutamate excitotoxicity, yet the precise requirement for synaptic glutamate release remains untested using genetic approaches. Here, we investigated noise-induced cochlear damage using Vglut3 knockout (Vglut3-KO) mice, which lack glutamatergic transmission from inner hair cells. Following 116 dB SPL noise exposure, wild-type (WT) mice exhibited permanent threshold shifts, persistent ABR wave I amplitude reduction, and significant loss of both ribbon synapses and outer hair cells (OHC) in the basal turn. Unexpectedly, Vglut3-KO mice also exhibited significant synapse loss despite their inability to release glutamate, revealing glutamate-independent mechanisms of synaptopathy. Proteomic analysis of noise-exposed cochleae identified 62 differentially expressed proteins enriched in synaptic and extracellular matrix pathways, including upregulation of Rps6ka1, Cplx2, and Cdk5, and downregulation of Ppa2. Comparative profiling of Vglut3-KO mice further revealed 233 differentially expressed proteins, with widespread downregulation of synaptic, mitochondrial, and ECM pathways. Importantly, noise exposure severely compromised AAV8-Vglut3 gene therapy efficacy in Vglut3-KO mice: while unexposed mutants achieved complete functional recovery, noise-exposed animals failed to attain normal hearing thresholds, with VGLUT3 expression restored across all cochlear turns as confirmed by immunofluorescence. These findings demonstrate that high-intensity noise induces synaptopathy through both excitotoxic and non-excitotoxic mechanisms involving synaptic and ECM disruption, and that acoustic trauma creates persistent OHC loss limiting gene therapy outcomes, underscoring the need for comprehensive otoprotective strategies in hereditary deafness patients awaiting treatment.

title: Targeting the bad neighbors: Precision nanotherapy for the adipose stromal niche
Exploring the therapeutic potential of human iPSC-NPC-based therapy in MPS IIIA
Host factor IRS4 impairs antitumor efficacy of oncolytic alphavirus via proteasomal viral protein degradation
abstract: Alphavirus M1, currently in phase I/II clinical trials (NCT07093814), provides a tractable system to define host determinants of oncolytic virus replication and efficacy. Tandem affinity purification-mass spectrometry mapped the nsP2 interactome in HEK293 cells and identified insulin receptor substrate 4 (IRS4) as a host restriction factor. Knockdown and reciprocal overexpression showed that IRS4 suppresses M1 replication and cytolysis without affecting baseline cell viability. Mechanistically, IRS4 engages the nsP23 replicase polyprotein in cells through an interaction interface mapped to the nsP2 C-domain and promotes ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation of nsP23, thereby attenuating nsP3-dependent subgenomic RNA synthesis and viral structural protein production. TCGA profiling revealed heterogeneous IRS4 elevation in subsets of tumors, suggesting that endogenous IRS4 status may influence responses to M1 virotherapy. Across 12 human cancer cell lines, higher IRS4 expression showed a nonsignificant trend toward reduced M1 sensitivity, with higher logIC50 and AUC values. In PC9 and UMUC3 cells, ectopic IRS4 expression impaired M1-mediated killing in vitro and abrogated antitumor efficacy in xenograft models. Together, these findings identify IRS4 as a regulator of M1 replicase stability and support the hypothesis that IRS4 expression may represent a candidate negative biomarker for M1 oncolytic virotherapy.

title: De Novo Structural Mining and Engineering of TadA Deaminases for High Efficiency Adenine Base Editors
abstract: Conventional enzyme discovery relies primarily on sequence homology and phylogenetic relationships, limiting the identification of functionally related but sequence-divergent proteins. Here, we developed a structure-guided mining framework integrating AlphaFold2-predicted structures with Foldseek-based three-dimensional alignment to identify previously uncharacterized TadA scaffolds with conserved folds and divergent sequences. Two candidates, eMaTadA and eErTadA, were engineered into functional adenine base editors (ABEs) by fusion to Cas9 nickase. The resulting editors mediated robust A-to-G editing with high product purity and restricted bystander editing. Under expression-stratified and activity-matched conditions, eMa-ABE and eEr-ABE showed reduced guide-dependent DNA off-target editing relative to ABE8e, while orthogonal R-loop assays revealed lower SpCas9-independent deamination of exposed ssDNA. In human CD34 + hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, eMa-ABE achieved up to approximately 80% editing at established HBG1/2 promoter targets and induced fetal hemoglobin expression following erythroid differentiation. Lipid nanoparticle delivery corrected approximately 50% of ATP7B P992L alleles in mouse liver, with no detectable increase in editing at the examined computationally predicted off-target loci. Furthermore, embedding eMaTadA within Cas9 expanded the editing window from A3-A9 to A3-A14 and enabled efficient start-codon-mediated gene inactivation. Collectively, this study establishes a structure-guided strategy for discovering and engineering sequence-divergent deaminases and expands the molecular diversity and therapeutic potential of the ABE toolkit.

title: A Combinatorial mRNA Therapy for Treating Rheumatoid Arthritis and Osteoarthritis by Inhibiting Inflammation and Preventing Cartilage Degeneration
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and osteoarthritis (OA) are debilitating joint disorders with distinct etiologies but share common pathological features of chronic inflammation and progressive cartilage damage. Current therapeutic options are largely palliative and yet fail to achieve desired effect. In this study, we developed a combinatorial mRNA therapy using a rationally engineered lipid nanoparticle (LNP) containing a novel ionizable lipid for enhanced cartilage penetration upon intra-articular administration. This LNP co-delivers mRNAs encoding two complementary therapeutic proteins: interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) for inflammation attenuation and a C-terminal truncated derivative of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANL3) for cartilage degeneration prevention. In pre-clinical models including collagen-induced arthritis mice, TNF-transgenic mice with spontaneous RA and destabilization of medial meniscus (DMM) surgical OA model, this dual therapy significantly ameliorated disease severity, reduced synovitis and bone erosion, and potently repaired cartilage damage. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling of joint specimens revealed that the combinatorial therapy concurrently suppressed inflammatory pathways and extracellular matrix degradation pathways, meanwhile upregulating anabolic genes facilitating chondrogenesis. Collectively, our study establishes a versatile and synergistic mRNA therapy that offers a potent disease-modifying immunomodulatory strategy capable of addressing the long-standing unmet needs in arthritis treatment.

title: Closed-loop inhibitory metabotropic glutamate receptor gene therapy for focal refractory epilepsy
abstract: Epilepsy is common and frequently refractory to anti-seizure medications. Although ablative surgery is effective when a seizure focus is identifiable, it is only suitable for a minority of patients because of risks of permanent neurological deficit. Several gene therapies for pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy are in development, including tools to achieve neuronal inhibition in response to pathological hyperactivity. Here we show that AAV9-mediated overexpression of the endogenous autoinhibitory metabotropic glutamate receptor mGlu2 (mGluR2, encoded by GRM2) prevents neuronal circuit hyperactivity ex vivo. Overexpression of mGlu2 in the ventral hippocampus suppressed chemoconvulsant-evoked seizures without affecting locomotion or behavioral markers of anxiety in naïve C57BL/6J mice. In a chronic model of pharmacoresistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, mGlu2 gene therapy profoundly attenuated spontaneous generalized seizures with no loss of efficacy over 8 weeks, and with concomitant improvements in comorbidities and survival. mGlu2 gene therapy avoids shortcomings of other strategies to suppress pathological hyperactivity in closed loop, relies on a mammalian effector transgene, and may thus be suitable for clinical translation.

title: A Scalable, Antibody-Free Lipid Nanoparticle Achieves Preferential mRNA Delivery to Human HSPCs In Vivo Without Conditioning
abstract: HSPCs, resulting in efficient gene editing and reduced β2M expression. These findings establish a ligand-free platform for functional RNA delivery and genome engineering in human HSPCs.

title: CochleaNet: deep learning-based image analysis for cochlear connectomics and gene therapy
abstract: With the emergence of gene and optogenetic therapies targeting deafness, the comprehensive analysis of the molecular anatomy and physiology of the cochlea has become ever more important. Here, we introduce CochleaNet, a deep learning-based framework to analyze volumetric imaging data obtained by light-sheet microscopy of decalcified, cleared and fluorescently labeled cochleae. CochleaNet covers the workflow from reconstruction of the cochlea to segmentation of inner hair cells, spiral ganglion neurons and their afferent synapses, to the analysis of tonotopy and specific fluorescent expression patterns. We validated CochleaNet by comparison to manual image analysis, also demonstrating its superiority to prior segmentation methods. We then analyzed different spiral ganglion neuron types and validated different gene therapy products with CochleaNet. Trained on high isotropic resolution mouse data, CochleaNet was also applicable to the cochlea of the gerbil, another relevant animal model, and lower-resolution mouse and marmoset data from a commercially available microscope. We conclude that the combination of light-sheet microscopy and image analysis with CochleaNet paves the way for rapid and reliable quantification of cochlear molecular anatomy and preclinical gene therapy outcomes.

Absence of Hepatobiliary Toxicity in Large Animal Species Dosed with AAV8 Gene Therapy for X-linked Myotubular Myopathy
abstract: X-linked myotubular myopathy (XLMTM) is caused by mutations in the MTM1 gene that encodes the myotubularin protein, essential for normal muscle development and function. XLMTM manifests as profound muscle weakness and hypotonia at birth, leading to severe respiratory insufficiency, and in many cases, early death. Resamirigene bilparvovec (rAAV8-Des-hMTM1) is a muscle-directed, adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based gene therapy in clinical development for the treatment of XLMTM. In the first-in-human clinical trial (ASPIRO; NCT03199469), rAAV8-Des-hMTM1 was associated with reduced ventilator dependence and unprecedented improvements in motor function in boys with XLMTM. However, four of the 24 participants who received rAAV8-Des-hMTM1 died after developing cholestatic liver failure. Safety results from large-animal studies of rAAV8-Des-MTM1 are presented herein and discussed retrospectively in the context of the adverse events observed in the clinical trial. Healthy infant cynomolgus monkeys and juvenile XLMTM dogs received relatively high doses of rAAV8-Des-hMTM1, or its canine version (rAAV8-Des-cMTM1), respectively. In both species, vector genomes were highest in liver, while myotubularin expression was highest in cardiac or skeletal muscle. rAAV8-Des-MTM1 was generally well-tolerated; importantly, there was no evidence of hyperbilirubinemia or other liver-associated toxicity following rAAV8-Des-MTM1 administration to cynomolgus monkeys or XLMTM dogs.

title: AAV-mediated Modulation of Dorsal Raphe Serotonergic Neurons Recapitulates Fenfluramine Efficacy in a Rat Model of Dravet Syndrome
abstract: rat model of DS, we demonstrate that chronic FFA treatment reduces the frequency of hyperthermia-induced seizures and attenuates pathological EEG network hypersynchrony. Furthermore, FFA administration ameliorates hyperactivity and depressive-like comorbidities, an effect associated with a marked reduction in hippocampal neuroinflammation and microglial overactivation. Transcriptomic analysis implicated serotonergic signaling in the therapeutic response to FFA, and subsequent anatomical and functional analyses revealed enhanced activity of dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) serotonergic neurons following FFA treatment. Cell-type-specific AAV-mediated modulation of DRN serotonergic neurons was sufficient to reproduce the key antiseizure and electrophysiological effects of FFA. Together, our findings identify the DRN serotonergic circuit as a therapeutically relevant circuit and provide proof-of-concept for mechanism-driven, circuit-specific neuromodulation strategies for Dravet syndrome.
